content: Naphtha is a hydrocarbon mixture that is derived from natural gas condensate, petroleum distillation, coal tar, or peat. It is a broad term encompassing some of the lightest and most volatile liquid hydrocarbon fractions found in petroleum. Naphtha appears as a colorless to reddish-brown volatile aromatic liquid, closely resembling gasoline in its properties. In petroleum engineering, full-range naphtha refers to the fraction of hydrocarbons in petroleum that boils between 30°C and 200°C. This fraction is composed of a complex mixture of hydrocarbon molecules, typically containing between 5 and 12 carbon atoms. Naphtha generally constitutes 15–30% of crude oil by weight. Light naphtha boils between 30°C and 90°C and consists of molecules with 5–6 carbon atoms, while heavy naphtha boils between 90°C and 200°C and contains molecules with 6–12 carbon atoms. Naphtha is primarily used as a feedstock for producing high-octane gasoline through catalytic reforming. It is also utilized in the bitumen mining industry as a diluent, in the petrochemical industry for producing olefins in steam crackers, and in the chemical industry for solvent applications such as cleaning. Common products made with naphtha include lighter fluid, fuel for camp stoves, and certain cleaning solvents. The term naphtha has its etymological roots in Latin and Greek, originating from the Persian language. In ancient Greek, it referred to any form of petroleum or pitch. The word appears in Arabic as nafţ (نَفْط) and in Hebrew as neft (נֵפְט), both meaning petroleum. Historical accounts indicate that Arabs and Persians distilled petroleum for tar and fuel in ancient times. The word naphtha is also mentioned in the Septuagint, where it is described as a miraculous flammable liquid. The term is the root of related words such as naphthalene and napalm, the latter derived from naphthenic acid and palmitic acid. From a health and safety perspective, certain forms of naphtha may be carcinogenic. Products sold as naphtha often contain impurities that may have harmful properties. As a product of the refining process, naphtha consists of a complex mixture of chemicals, making it challenging to identify specific carcinogens. Acute exposure to naphtha can cause symptoms such as dizziness, narcosis, and loss of consciousness. Chronic exposure may lead to toxic encephalopathy, categorized by the World Health Organization into reversible symptoms (Type 1), mild chronic encephalopathy (Type 2), and severe chronic toxic encephalopathy (Type 3). Topical exposure can result in a burning sensation on the skin, followed by contact dermatitis. Naphtha is highly volatile and can explode when exposed to high-temperature surfaces. For example, an explosion involving naphtha at the Avon Refinery in California in 1999 resulted in four fatalities. Its molecular weight ranges from 100 to 215 g/mol, with a density of 750–785 kg/m³ and a boiling point of 160–220°C. Naphtha is insoluble in water and incompatible with strong oxidizers. In petroleum refineries, naphtha is obtained as an intermediate product during the distillation of crude oil. It serves as a liquid intermediate between the light gases and heavier kerosene fractions. Naphtha types are distinguished by their density and chemical composition, including paraffins, isoparaffins, olefins, naphthenes, and aromatics. Parafinnic naphthas, which are less dense, are primarily used as feedstock in the petrochemical production of olefins. Heavier naphthas, richer in naphthenes and aromatics, are often used in catalytic reformers to produce high-octane reformate. Naphtha has various applications, including as an unprocessed component in motor gasoline production, industrial solvents, cleaning fluids, and lighter fluids. It is also used as a fuel for portable stoves and lanterns, as well as in fire performance equipment. Historically, naphtha was likely an ingredient in Greek fire and was used in medieval battles as a primitive grenade. In the furniture industry, it is employed to temporarily reveal the patina of wood during finishing processes. Examples of naphtha in daily life include products like Shellite (Australia), also known as white gas or Coleman fuel in North America. Shellite is a highly flammable liquid with a low flash point, making it suitable for use in low-pressure camping stoves. It is also a fast-drying solvent used for cleaning metal, hard plastic, and painted surfaces.
